paras: The killing of Richard Smith took place on May 23, 1903, at the Mobile Lumber Company's mill outside Mobile, Alabama, where Smith, a Black employee, was cut to death after a dispute over his pay with the company's white owner, Marion L. Daugherty, and an employee, H. Ross Rogers. Daugherty and Rogers were charged with murder, and Black co-workers testified that Daugherty had called for Smith's death and fired a pistol at him as he fled. A grand jury did not indict Daugherty, and in July a jury acquitted Rogers of manslaughter on a plea of self-defense.

Daugherty was senior owner and president of the Mobile Lumber Company, a hardwood plant on the Louisville and Nashville Railroad about half a mile north of One Mile Creek, and Rogers was one of his employees. According to Dan Morisette, who was in the office, Smith told Daugherty that his time was wrong and, after saying something about the law, was ordered out.

John Reed, who was with Smith at the office window, testified that Rogers jumped off the gallery and struck Smith, who struck back, and that Daugherty rose and said "let's kill the," a word the newspaper left blank. As Smith walked away, Daugherty struck or threw a stick at him, and Rogers followed him to the railroad, where the two men clinched. In the first account, given by Black eyewitnesses, Rogers used a knife that severed the femoral artery in one of Smith's legs and cut his legs in other places.

Men nearby had been practicing with a pistol, and Daugherty took it and ran toward the fight. Smith broke away and ran down the track; a shot was heard, and after running the distance of two telegraph poles he fell and died. Bollie Williams testified that the pistol "appeared to me" to be aimed at Smith, and Alex Reed said Daugherty told him afterward that he had shot only to scare Smith, who "wasn't shot, he was cut."

Deputy Murphy arrested Rogers when the two men came into the city by launch, and Daugherty was arrested at the sheriff's office. A coroner's inquest recommended holding Rogers, and on May 25 Judge Jules E. Alford heard the case against Daugherty, Rogers and a third white man, Jack Strong; twenty Black witnesses attended. Alford discharged Strong and held Daugherty and Rogers without bond for the grand jury.

At a habeas corpus hearing on May 30, Judge Price Williams admitted Daugherty to bail at $5,000 and remanded Rogers. The grand jury failed to indict Daugherty, and Rogers, charged with manslaughter, was bailed at $5,000. Rogers was tried in the City Court in mid-July, and the jury acquitted him after twenty-three minutes.

The only coverage found is a series of five reports from the Mobile bureau of the Montgomery Advertiser, running from May 24 to July 17; no Black newspaper coverage was found. The first report, headed "A CHARGE OF MURDER," said it was "Alleged That the Two White Men Were Instrumental in the Death of a Negro," on the word of "several negroes" who saw it. The hearing report printed both sides' testimony at length, with the final word of Daugherty's reported threat left blank, and remarked that "all of the witnesses for the defense were white" and that both defendants were "of prominent families."

By July the paper's account had shifted: under the headline "Rogers Was Acquitted," it did not name Smith, calling him only "a negro," and said it had been "proved" that Rogers was being beaten over the head with a rock or slag.

The Black witnesses said Rogers struck the first blow and that Daugherty's pistol was pointed at Smith's head, and Reed testified that Smith's hat bore a hole in court that it had not had when he last saw it. The white defense witnesses, C. J. Crow and Strong, said Smith struck Rogers with a rock "twice size of a man's hand" and that Daugherty fired over Smith's head, and a defense physician found two lumps on Rogers's head.
The habeas corpus report names the victim "Jacob Smith," and the July report places the mill on Three Mile Creek rather than near One Mile Creek.

reader.title: Killing of Richard Smith
bases: A white mill owner and his employee were charged with killing a Black employee of the Mobile Lumber Company after a dispute over his pay at the company office, not a posse or mob action (A1, A2, A3).

Smith was killed (A1, A2), but the papers name two assailants, Rogers with a knife and Daugherty with a pistol, acting in a workplace quarrel rather than a group of three or more acting under a pretext of justice or tradition; a third man charged, Strong, was discharged and testified he turned back (A3), and a jury found Rogers acted in self-defense (A6).

All five reports come from the Mobile bureau of the Montgomery Advertiser (A1, A2, A3, A4, A6); within them, sworn testimony from both Black and white witnesses agrees that Smith died of knife wounds after a fight with Rogers and that Daugherty fired a pistol (A2, A3).

accounts.label: Black eyewitnesses (first report and preliminary hearing)
accounts.gist: After a dispute over pay, Rogers attacked Smith, Daugherty called out to kill him and struck at him with a stick, Rogers overtook and cut him at the railroad, and Daugherty chased him and fired a pistol aimed at his head before he fell dead.

accounts.label: White defense witnesses
accounts.gist: Smith picked up a rock and beat Rogers about the head, and Daugherty fired over Smith's head; Strong denied handing Daugherty the pistol.

accounts.label: Daugherty, as reported by a witness
accounts.gist: According to Alex Reed, Daugherty said afterward that he had shot only to scare Smith and that Smith had been cut, not shot.

accounts.label: Trial jury
accounts.gist: The City Court jury accepted the defense that Rogers acted in self-defense and acquitted him.

framing.detail: The first headline, 'A CHARGE OF MURDER', said it was 'Alleged That the Two White Men Were Instrumental in the Death of a Negro'; the hearing report printed testimony from both sides at length.

The paper noted both defendants were 'of prominent families' and, in reporting the acquittal under the headline 'Rogers Was Acquitted', stated as fact that it was 'proved' Smith had been beating Rogers with a rock, without naming Smith.

versions.value: Rogers struck Smith first in the office yard, and Daugherty struck at him with a stick as he left
Smith picked up a rock and struck Rogers about the head; the jury found Rogers acted in self-defense

conflicts.note: The Black witnesses testified under oath at the preliminary hearing; the trial testimony was not printed, only the verdict and the Advertiser's summary of the defense.

versions.value: Daugherty chased Smith with the pistol pointed at his head, and a shot was heard before Smith fell; the hat shown in court had a hole the witness had not seen before

conflicts.note: Both sides agree the fatal wounds were knife cuts; the dispute is whether Daugherty fired at Smith.
